title: Terminal Classic Maya collapse
summary: Between about 800 and 950 CE many Classic Maya kingdoms, above all in the southern lowlands, lost their rulers, stopped raising monuments and were largely abandoned. Warfare, drought and political change are all argued; the decline was earlier and sharper in the south than in the north.

uncertainty.note: One source gives the Terminal Classic as about 800-950 CE; another gives the decline as 800-900/1000 CE. Timing varies by site, and drought episodes in a northern cave record run 871-1021 CE.

as_recorded.value: severe dry spells between 871 and 1021 CE, the period called the Terminal Classic

where.modern_name: Reference point: Tikal, Peten, Guatemala, in the southern Maya lowlands (the collapse spans the southern and northern lowlands of Mexico, Guatemala, Belize and Honduras)
where.historical_name: Classic Maya lowland kingdoms (e.g. Tikal, Calakmul), Late/Terminal Classic

importance.justification: One of the best-known episodes of political collapse and regional depopulation in world history, central to debates about climate and societal resilience.

related.because: Late Classic population pressure, warfare and drought undermined the southern kingdoms (per the existing period outline).

sources.title: Drought, agricultural adaptation, and sociopolitical collapse in the Maya Lowlands (PNAS 112:5607-5612)
sources.publisher: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (via PubMed Central)
sources.author: Peter M. J. Douglas, Mark Pagani, Marcello A. Canuto, Mark Brenner, David A. Hodell, Timothy I. Eglinton, Jason H. Curtis

sources.title: Ancient cave clues reveal secrets of the Maya civilisation collapse

reviewer_note: Least sure of the single pin: the collapse is regional; Tikal is only a reference point in the southern lowlands (uncertainty set to 300 km). Cause is debated (drought, war, trade shifts); the summary does not assert one cause.
